turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I suppose I’m here because... it’s this whole situation with my kitchen. For nearly two years now, I’ve been absolutely sure that our contractor and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. They're keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. Which is such a shame because I picked out this beautiful butter-yellow paint for the walls. I actually got the idea from a magazine I was reading at my dentist's office. Dr. Miller, over on 4th Street. He’s a wonderful dentist, though his waiting room is always freezing. I always have to bring my thick wool cardigan when I go for a cleaning. The one my daughter knitted for me—she lives in Seattle now, you know, and it rains so much there she just knits all the time. 

But anyway, my husband keeps showing me all these receipts and giving me their excuses, but it doesn't change what I know is going on. I know they're leaving it wrong on purpose.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient holds a fixed belief that her contractor and neighbors are conspiring to cheat her, which she maintains despite her husband showing her contradictory evidence like receipts.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and derailment, wandering from her kitchen to paint colors, her dentist's office, a wool cardigan, and her daughter in Seattle before returning to the main topic.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear?
turns.patient_response: No, no, I've never had anything like that happen. My hearing is actually quite good for my age. Better than my husband's, that's for sure. He has the television turned up so loud in the evenings, it's a wonder the whole neighborhood doesn't complain. We usually watch those trivia game shows after dinner. I'm actually quite good at them, especially the history questions. I always loved history in high school. Mr. Henderson was my teacher, and he had this fascinating way of talking about the Revolutionary War. He used to wear these tweed jackets with the little patches on the elbows. You don't see those much anymore, do you? It's a shame, I think they look very distinguished. But no, to answer your question, no voices or anything like that. Just the television being too loud.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or sounds that others cannot hear.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't. I'm actually quite healthy. I just had my annual check-up a few months ago with Dr. Evans, and he said my chart looks wonderful. His office is right next to that new garden center on Route 9, actually. I stopped in there right after my appointment because I’ve been trying to find some decent marigolds for the front porch planters. The deer just absolutely destroyed my hostas last year. They come right up into the yard at dusk, bold as brass, looking for a snack. My neighbor, Susan—she’s the one with those terrible bright pink shutters, I really don't know what she was thinking with that color—she tried putting out this spray that smells like rotten eggs to keep the deer away. It smelled so awful we couldn't even sit on our patio for a week! We had to eat all our dinners inside with the windows shut. It was right during that heatwave in July, too. But anyway, no, my brain and my body are perfectly fine. No conditions like that.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a very long, rambling, and overly detailed response to a simple yes/no question, demonstrating excessive talking.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, drifting from the doctor's office to a garden center, deer, a neighbor's shutters, and a heatwave before finally returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever felt like someone or something outside of yourself was putting thoughts into your head or controlling your mind?
turns.patient_response: No, I've never felt anything like that. My mind is my own, thank goodness. I've always been very independent-minded. Even when I was a little girl, my mother used to say I was stubborn as a mule. She grew up on a farm, you know, out in Iowa. They actually had mules! And chickens, and dairy cows. She used to tell me stories about getting up before the sun to milk the cows. I can't even imagine. I'm definitely not a morning person. My husband is, though. He's up at five-thirty every single day, clattering around in the kitchen—well, what's left of the kitchen, anyway. He makes his coffee in that French press contraption. It seems like so much work for one cup of coffee, and the glass is so fragile. He broke the first one we had while he was washing it, just tapped it against the side of the sink and it shattered everywhere. We were finding little pieces of glass on the floor for weeks, no matter how many times I swept. I had to buy a special attachment for the vacuum cleaner just to be sure. It was on sale at the hardware store, the one downtown that still has the creaky wooden floors. I just love the smell of that place, like sawdust and machine oil. But no, nobody is putting thoughts in my head. Just my own thoughts in there.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits tangentiality, wandering through loosely connected topics (mules, mother's farm, husband's coffee, broken glass, hardware store) before returning to the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies experiencing thought insertion or mind control, stating her mind is her own and nobody is putting thoughts in her head.
